question: Hawaii is unusual among U.S. states because real property may be held under either of two separate title systems. What are these two systems?
choice_a: The county recorder system and the state assessor system
choice_b: The MLS system and the escrow system
choice_c: The federal patent system and the state patent system
choice_d: The regular system (Bureau of Conveyances recording) and the Land Court (Torrens) registration system
explanation: Hawaii property may be recorded under the 'regular system' (HRS Chapter 502, Bureau of Conveyances) or registered under the Land Court/Torrens system (HRS Chapter 501) — a genuinely distinctive dual-system structure. The county recorder/state assessor pairing, MLS/escrow pairing, and dual patent system in the other choices are not real Hawaii title systems.
source_note: HRS Chapters 501 & 502; Hawaii Bureau of Conveyances (ags.hawaii.gov/boc)

question: A Hawaii broker is preparing to list a property and needs to determine whether the parcel is in the regular system or the Land Court system. What is the most reliable way to make this determination?
choice_a: Review the property's title report or Bureau of Conveyances records, which will show either a recorded document number or a Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) number
choice_b: Ask the seller which system they prefer
choice_c: Assume all single-family homes are Land Court and all condominiums are regular system
choice_d: Check the county real property tax assessment notice only
explanation: A title report or a Bureau of Conveyances search identifies a document/book-page reference for regular-system land or a TCT number for Land Court land. System membership is not a matter of seller preference, is not correlated with property type as claimed, and is not shown definitively by a tax notice alone.
source_note: Bureau of Conveyances Document Search and Ordering system; HRS Chapters 501 & 502

question: Under Hawaii's regular recording system (HRS Chapter 502), where must a deed conveying real property be recorded to provide constructive notice to third parties?
choice_a: With the county recorder in the county where the property is located
choice_b: With the State Bureau of Conveyances, Hawaii's single statewide recording office
choice_c: With the Hawaii Association of Realtors
choice_d: With the Real Estate Branch of the Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs
explanation: Hawaii has no county recorders; the Bureau of Conveyances is the sole statewide recording office for regular-system documents — Hawaii is reputedly the only state with this centralized structure. The county-recorder option is wrong precisely because Hawaii lacks that office, and the Realtor association and DCCA's Real Estate Branch are not recording offices.
source_note: HRS Chapter 502; Bureau of Conveyances (ags.hawaii.gov/boc)

question: Hawaii's recording statute, HRS section 502-83, follows a 'race-notice' rule. Under this rule, an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later purchaser who...
choice_a: simply records first, regardless of notice or good faith
choice_b: has actual notice of the prior unrecorded conveyance but records first anyway
choice_c: takes in good faith, for valuable consideration, without actual notice of the prior conveyance, and records first
choice_d: purchases the property at any price and records within one year
explanation: Race-notice protects a subsequent purchaser only if all elements are met: good faith, valuable consideration, no actual notice of the earlier conveyance, AND recording first. A pure 'first to record wins' rule (regardless of notice) describes a different type of statute, not Hawaii's; actual notice of the prior conveyance defeats protection no matter the recording order.

question: Hawaii's Land Court, which administers the Torrens-style land registration system, was established under HRS Chapter 501 in...
choice_a: 1959, at statehood
choice_b: 1978, following the state constitutional convention
choice_c: 1850, under the Kuleana Act
choice_d: 1903, by the Territorial Legislature
explanation: The Hawaii Land Court and its registration system were created in 1903 by the Territorial Legislature (Act 56), predating statehood by over 50 years. Statehood (1959) and the 1978 constitutional convention are unrelated dates for this purpose, and the Kuleana Act (1850) addressed native tenant land claims, not Torrens registration.
source_note: HRS Chapter 501; Hawaii Land Court history

question: In Hawaii's Land Court system, once land is registered, the Certificate of Title issued for it is best described as...
choice_a: conclusive and unimpeachable as to the matters it contains, subject to limited statutory exceptions
choice_b: advisory only, subject to being overridden by any unrecorded claim
choice_c: valid for five years before requiring renewal
choice_d: identical in legal effect to a private abstract of title from a title company
explanation: A Land Court Certificate of Title is conclusive and unimpeachable, offering a far stronger title guarantee than the regular system's recorded chain of title. It does not merely serve as advice that any unrecorded claim can override, it does not expire and require renewal, and it is a government-issued instrument distinct from a private title company's abstract.
source_note: HRS Chapter 501; Hawaii Land Court practice

question: How does Hawaii's Land Court (Torrens) registration affect a claim of adverse possession?
choice_a: Adverse possession works the same on Land Court land as on regular-system land
choice_b: Adverse possession is not possible against land registered in the Land Court system
choice_c: Adverse possession requires only 5 years on Land Court land, versus 20 years on regular-system land
choice_d: Adverse possession can only be claimed against Land Court land by a government entity
explanation: A key protection of Torrens registration is that registered title is indefeasible against adverse possession — a squatter cannot acquire title to Land Court property no matter how long they occupy it, which is precisely why the systems are treated differently. Claiming the rule is identical to the regular system, or inventing a shortened time period or a government-only carve-out, misstates this protection.
source_note: HRS Chapter 501; Hawaii Land Court practice

question: For land registered in Hawaii's Land Court, when does legal title actually transfer to a grantee?
choice_a: Upon signing of the deed by the grantor
choice_b: Upon delivery of the deed to the grantee, the same rule as regular-system property
choice_c: Upon registration of the transfer instrument with the Land Court, noted on the Certificate of Title
choice_d: Upon payment of the state conveyance tax
explanation: For Land Court property, registration — not delivery — is the operative act that transfers title, and the transfer must be noted on the Certificate of Title to be effective. The 'delivery' rule is the common-law rule that governs regular-system deeds, and it does not apply to registered land; mere signing or tax payment does not itself transfer title.
source_note: HRS Chapter 501

question: A mortgage is executed against a parcel registered in Hawaii's Land Court system. For the mortgage to affect the registered land, what must occur?
choice_a: The mortgage must be recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances regular system, exactly as with unregistered land
choice_b: Nothing further is required once the mortgage is signed and notarized
choice_c: The mortgage must be published in a newspaper of general circulation
choice_d: The mortgage must be memorialized and noted on the property's Certificate of Title through the Land Court
explanation: Encumbrances on Land Court property — mortgages, leases, liens, judgments — must be noted on the Certificate of Title to affect the land; simply recording in the regular system, without more, does not bind registered land. Signing and notarizing alone is insufficient, and newspaper publication is not part of the process.
source_note: HRS Chapter 501; Bureau of Conveyances, Land Court Division

question: Who is responsible for maintaining Certificates of Title and processing filings against registered land in Hawaii's Land Court?
choice_a: The Assistant Registrar of the Land Court
choice_b: The County Recorder
choice_c: The Real Estate Commission
choice_d: The Director of Taxation
explanation: The Land Court is administered by a Registrar/Assistant Registrar, housed within the Bureau of Conveyances, who maintains Certificates of Title and processes registered-land filings. Hawaii has no county recorders, and the Real Estate Commission and the Department of Taxation play no role in this function.
source_note: HRS Chapter 501

question: Contested matters requiring judicial determination in Hawaii's Land Court, such as an original application for registration, are heard by...
choice_a: A panel of three Bureau of Conveyances examiners
choice_b: A judge of the First Circuit Court assigned to sit as the Land Court judge
choice_c: The Hawaii Real Estate Commission
choice_d: A federal district court judge
explanation: The Land Court is a specialized part of the state judiciary; a judge of the Circuit Court of the First Circuit is assigned to hear Land Court matters, including original registration applications. There is no panel of Bureau of Conveyances examiners with judicial authority, the Real Estate Commission is a licensing body, and federal courts have no role in Land Court registration.
source_note: HRS Chapter 501

question: Nearly every Hawaii real estate document — deeds, listings, title reports — references a parcel identifier unique to the state. What is it called?
choice_a: The Assessor Parcel Number (APN)
choice_b: The Legal Lot Index (LLI)
choice_c: The Tax Map Key (TMK)
choice_d: The County Grid Reference (CGR)
explanation: Hawaii uses the Tax Map Key (TMK) system to identify every parcel statewide, used across county tax offices, title reports, and Bureau of Conveyances document searches. The Assessor Parcel Number is the term used in most other states, not Hawaii, and the other two labels are not real Hawaii designations.
source_note: County Real Property Assessment Divisions; Bureau of Conveyances Document Search system

question: Hawaii's Bureau of Conveyances document search system allows the public to search recorded and registered documents. Besides grantor/grantee name, by what two parcel-specific identifiers can a search typically be run?
choice_a: Zip code and lot size
choice_b: MLS number and school district
choice_c: Census tract and flood zone
choice_d: TMK (Tax Map Key) and TCT (Transfer Certificate of Title) number
explanation: Bureau of Conveyances records can be searched by TMK, applicable to either title system, or by TCT number specifically for Land Court parcels — directly reflecting the dual-system structure. Zip code/lot size, MLS number/school district, and census tract/flood zone are not identifiers the Bureau of Conveyances search uses.
source_note: Bureau of Conveyances Document Search and Ordering system

question: Hawaii has historically had an unusually large share of real property held under long-term ground leases rather than fee simple ownership. In a typical Hawaii ground lease arrangement, a buyer purchases...
choice_a: The leasehold interest and improvements, while a separate lessor retains fee title to the land, subject to periodic rent renegotiation
choice_b: Fee simple title but must pay an annual property tax surcharge
choice_c: A time-share interest limited to specific weeks of the year
choice_d: An easement only, with no right to occupy improvements
explanation: In a Hawaii ground lease, the buyer acquires the leasehold estate — typically owning the improvements — while a separate landowner-lessor retains the fee, with lease rent periodically renegotiated per the lease terms; this was historically a major feature of the Hawaii market before land-reform legislation expanded fee conversion. The buyer does not receive fee title, a time-share interest, or a bare easement.
source_note: General Hawaii leasehold market practice; HRS Chapter 516

question: Hawaii's Land Reform Act of 1967 (HRS Chapter 516) authorized the state to use eminent domain to acquire leased-fee interests in residential house lots and convey fee simple title to lessees. This program was challenged and ultimately upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in which case?
choice_a: Kelo v. City of New London
choice_b: Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff (1984)
choice_c: Palazzolo v. Rhode Island
choice_d: Loretto v. Teleprompter Manhattan CATV Corp.
explanation: In Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff, 467 U.S. 229 (1984), the U.S. Supreme Court upheld Hawaii's Land Reform Act, holding that redistributing concentrated fee ownership to lessees served a legitimate public purpose satisfying the Fifth Amendment's 'public use' requirement. Kelo is a later, different eminent domain case from Connecticut, and the other two cases address unrelated takings issues.
source_note: Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff, 467 U.S. 229 (1984); HRS Chapter 516

question: Which Hawaii statute specifically provides a mechanism for owners of leasehold condominium units to compel conversion of their leasehold interest to fee simple ownership?
choice_a: HRS Chapter 501
choice_b: HRS Chapter 507
choice_c: HRS Chapter 514C
choice_d: HRS Chapter 502
explanation: HRS Chapter 514C provides Hawaii's leasehold condominium lease-to-fee conversion process, distinct from Chapter 516 (which applies to single-family residential house lots). Chapters 501, 507, and 502 instead govern Land Court registration, liens, and Bureau of Conveyances recording, and do not address leasehold condominium conversion.
source_note: HRS Chapter 514C

question: A Hawaii broker representing a buyer interested in a condominium unit discovers that no statutory right currently exists for that specific building's leasehold owners to force conversion to fee simple. What should the broker do?
choice_a: Assume HRS Chapter 516 will eventually apply and tell the buyer conversion is guaranteed
choice_b: Advise the buyer that all Hawaii leaseholds automatically convert to fee simple after 30 years
choice_c: Decline to discuss the leasehold status since it is a legal matter outside the broker's duties
choice_d: Disclose to the buyer that no assurance of mandatory leasehold-to-fee conversion currently applies to that property, and that lease terms (rent resets, expiration) should be carefully reviewed
explanation: Because leasehold condominiums have no guaranteed statutory conversion right absent an applicable Chapter 514C mechanism, a broker must disclose the leasehold nature and its risks, such as rent renegotiation and lease expiration, rather than assume conversion will occur, invent an automatic 30-year rule, or avoid the topic entirely, which would violate disclosure duties.
source_note: HRS Chapter 514C; general leasehold condominium disclosure practice

question: Under HRS Chapter 509, which of the following relationships may hold Hawaii real property as tenants by the entirety?
choice_a: Married spouses, registered civil union partners, and reciprocal beneficiaries
choice_b: Any two unrelated business partners
choice_c: Parent and adult child only
choice_d: Any co-owners who simply request that designation on a deed
explanation: HRS § 509-2 extends tenancy by the entirety not only to spouses under Chapter 572, but also to civil union partners under Chapter 572B and reciprocal beneficiaries under Chapter 572C. Unrelated business partners, a parent-child pair, or any co-owners generally do not qualify for this specific marital-type tenancy simply by requesting it.

question: One key legal advantage of holding Hawaii real property as tenants by the entirety, rather than tenants in common, is that...
choice_a: The property is exempt from all property taxes
choice_b: The property is immune from claims of a creditor of only one spouse, not both
choice_c: Either spouse may unilaterally sell their share without the other's consent
choice_d: The property automatically passes through probate rather than by survivorship
explanation: Under HRS Chapter 509, an estate by the entirety is protected from the separate creditors of just one spouse — a significant asset-protection feature that ends upon divorce, converting the tenancy to a tenancy in common. The property is not tax-exempt, one spouse cannot unilaterally convey entirety property (unlike tenancy in common), and it passes by right of survivorship rather than through probate.

question: Under HRS section 509-1, when a deed conveys Hawaii real property to two or more unmarried persons without specifying the form of co-ownership, how is the tenancy construed?
choice_a: As a joint tenancy with right of survivorship
choice_b: As a tenancy by the entirety
choice_c: As a tenancy in common
choice_d: As a tenancy in partnership
explanation: HRS § 509-1 provides that a conveyance to two or more persons is construed as creating a tenancy in common unless the instrument expressly states that a joint tenancy is intended. A joint tenancy requires express language to arise, tenancy by the entirety is limited to spouses, civil union partners, or reciprocal beneficiaries, and 'tenancy in partnership' is not the applicable default rule.

question: A contractor records a mechanic's lien against a Hawaii property under HRS Chapter 507 after completing unpaid work. For priority purposes, from what point does the lien take effect?
choice_a: The date the lien document is recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances
choice_b: The date the underlying contract was signed
choice_c: The date the certificate of occupancy is issued
choice_d: The date of visible commencement of operations for the improvement
explanation: Under HRS Chapter 507, a mechanic's or materialman's lien relates back to and takes effect from the time of visible commencement of operations on the improvement, not the later recording date, the earlier contract-signing date, or the occupancy date — this relation-back can give the lien priority over interests created after work began but before the lien was actually recorded.
source_note: HRS § 507-42 et seq.

question: Hawaii mechanic's and materialmen's liens generally have priority over other liens of any nature EXCEPT...
choice_a: Liens in favor of any government branch, and mortgages, liens, or judgments recorded or filed before visible commencement of operations
choice_b: Liens filed by other contractors on the same project
choice_c: Any lien recorded after the mechanic's lien, regardless of type
choice_d: Liens held by out-of-state creditors
explanation: HRS Chapter 507 gives mechanics' liens priority over most other liens, but not over government liens or mortgages, liens, and judgments already recorded or filed before visible commencement of work. Liens filed by other contractors on the same project actually rank equally among each other rather than defeating priority, and a lien recorded later or held by an out-of-state creditor is not itself a recognized exception under the statute.
source_note: HRS § 507-42 et seq.

question: A Hawaii general contractor asks a subcontractor to sign a waiver of lien rights before any work begins, as a condition of the contract. Is this waiver enforceable?
choice_a: Yes, if both parties are licensed contractors
choice_b: No — prospective lien waivers executed before work commences are void as against public policy under HRS Chapter 507
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial (not residential) projects
choice_d: No, unless the waiver is notarized and recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances
explanation: HRS § 507-42 voids prospective lien waivers signed before construction work commences, protecting subcontractors and suppliers regardless of licensing status or project type. Notarizing or recording such a prospective waiver would not cure the underlying statutory prohibition.

question: Real property tax liens imposed by a Hawaii county for unpaid property taxes are distinctive in that they...
choice_a: Must be recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances before they attach to the property
choice_b: Cannot be enforced unless the owner is also delinquent on the state conveyance tax
choice_c: Attach automatically by operation of law and generally take priority without needing to be recorded like a private lien
choice_d: Expire automatically after one year if unpaid
explanation: Like most government tax liens, Hawaii county real property tax liens attach automatically by statute and are typically given high priority without requiring recording in the way a private mortgage or judgment lien must be recorded to bind third parties. They do not require prior Bureau of Conveyances recording, they are unrelated to conveyance tax delinquency, and they do not simply expire after one year unpaid.
source_note: County real property tax lien statutes; general Hawaii lien priority practice

question: The Kuleana Act of 1850 is historically significant to Hawaii title and boundary issues because it...
choice_a: Established the Bureau of Conveyances
choice_b: Created Hawaii's mechanic's lien statute
choice_c: Abolished the ground lease system statewide
choice_d: Granted fee simple ownership to native Hawaiian tenant farmers for land they actively cultivated, creating small parcels (kuleana) that can still exist as inholdings within larger properties today
explanation: The Kuleana Act of 1850 allowed the Land Commission to award fee-simple kuleana parcels to native Hawaiian commoners who actively cultivated the land; these small kuleana parcels can still exist today as separately-titled inholdings within a larger surrounding property, a real and continuing source of boundary and access issues. It did not establish the Bureau of Conveyances, create the mechanic's lien statute, or abolish ground leases.
source_note: Kuleana Act of 1850; Hawaii land tenure history

question: A buyer is purchasing a large parcel that surrounds an older kuleana parcel owned by a different party. What boundary-related issue should the buyer's agent flag?
choice_a: The kuleana parcel may carry historic access, gathering, and water rights across the surrounding land, which can affect the larger parcel's use and boundaries
choice_b: The kuleana owner has no legal rights beyond the physical boundary of their small parcel
choice_c: Kuleana parcels automatically merge into the surrounding parcel after 50 years
choice_d: Kuleana designations only apply to commercial property
explanation: Kuleana lands can carry statutory access, gathering, and water rights, traditional customary rights that extend beyond the kuleana parcel's own boundary onto the surrounding land — a real and distinctive Hawaii title and boundary consideration for the owner of the surrounding property. The kuleana owner's rights are not confined to their own parcel boundary, kuleana parcels do not automatically merge into surrounding land, and the designation applies to residential/agricultural inholdings, not commercial property specifically.
source_note: Kuleana Act of 1850; Hawaii land tenure history

question: In Hawaii, a mortgagee seeking to foreclose on defaulted real property may generally choose between which two foreclosure methods?
choice_a: Tax sale foreclosure or lien-stripping foreclosure
choice_b: Judicial foreclosure through the courts, or nonjudicial (power of sale) foreclosure under HRS Chapter 667
choice_c: Land Court foreclosure or Bureau of Conveyances foreclosure
choice_d: Arbitration-based foreclosure or mediation-based foreclosure
explanation: Hawaii is one of the relatively few states permitting both judicial foreclosure, which is court-supervised, and nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure under HRS Chapter 667, subject to procedural requirements and, for owner-occupants, conversion rights. Tax sale/lien-stripping, Land Court/Bureau of Conveyances, and arbitration/mediation-based foreclosure are not recognized methods under Hawaii law.
source_note: HRS Chapter 667

question: Under Hawaii's foreclosure statutes, an owner-occupant facing a nonjudicial (power of sale) foreclosure on their primary residence has the right to...
choice_a: automatically stop the foreclosure permanently by filing any objection
choice_b: demand the lender waive the entire debt
choice_c: convert the nonjudicial foreclosure to a judicial foreclosure by filing the required form with the circuit court within 30 days after being served notice
choice_d: require the lender to sell the property at a price set by the owner
explanation: An owner-occupant, meaning the property has been their primary residence for at least 200 days before notice, may convert a nonjudicial foreclosure to a judicial one by timely filing the statutory form with the circuit court within 30 days of service, allowing claims and defenses to be heard by a judge. The statute does not grant a right to permanently stop foreclosure by any objection, to demand full debt forgiveness, or to dictate the sale price.
source_note: HRS Chapter 667 (owner-occupant foreclosure notice and conversion provisions)

question: Following a completed nonjudicial (power of sale) foreclosure against an owner-occupant's primary residence in Hawaii, can the lender obtain a deficiency judgment against the owner-occupant for any shortfall?
choice_a: Yes, deficiency judgments are always permitted after any Hawaii foreclosure
choice_b: Yes, but only if the property sold for less than half its appraised value
choice_c: No, deficiency judgments are prohibited after every type of Hawaii foreclosure, judicial or nonjudicial
choice_d: No — deficiency judgments against an owner-occupant are generally prohibited after a nonjudicial foreclosure, unless the debt is secured by other collateral
explanation: Hawaii law generally bars a deficiency judgment against an owner-occupant after a nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure, unless other collateral secures the debt, while judicial foreclosure may still permit the lender to seek a deficiency judgment — a meaningful distinction between the two paths. Claiming deficiency judgments are always available, or that they are barred after every type of foreclosure, or that a specific sale-price threshold controls, all misstate this rule.
source_note: HRS Chapter 667

question: Act 48, Session Laws of Hawaii 2011, significantly reformed Hawaii foreclosure law. Among its provisions was a temporary measure that...
choice_a: imposed a temporary moratorium on new nonjudicial (power of sale) foreclosures and created a mortgage foreclosure dispute resolution program
choice_b: eliminated nonjudicial foreclosure permanently statewide
choice_c: required all foreclosures to be handled exclusively by the Land Court
choice_d: abolished mechanic's liens on residential property
explanation: Act 48 (2011) temporarily halted new nonjudicial foreclosures under HRS Chapter 667 Part I and gave owner-occupants access to a mortgage foreclosure dispute resolution program, rather than eliminating nonjudicial foreclosure permanently or shifting foreclosure jurisdiction to the Land Court, and it had nothing to do with mechanic's liens.
source_note: Act 48, Session Laws of Hawaii 2011; HRS Chapter 667
